chapter_mapping: Chapter C3 Chemicals of the natural environment plus chapter C4 Material choices, confirmed against the lesson content: L1 = C3.2 (reactivity and extraction), L2 = C3.3 (electrolysis), L3 = C3.4 (crude oil, alkanes, cracking, combustion), L4 = C4.2 with parts of C4.1 and C4.3 (polymers), L5 = C4.4 and C4.5 (nanoparticles, LCA, end of life). C3.1 (metallic bonding) is taught in the atoms-patterns-bonding unit, not here. J258 has eight teaching chapters C1-C8, with C7 Ideas about Science and C8 Practical Skills.
assessment_structure: Four externally assessed components. Breadth in chemistry = 01 Foundation and 03 Higher; Depth in chemistry = 02 Foundation and 04 Higher. Each is 90 marks, 1 hour 45 minutes, 50% of that tier. Both Breadth and Depth assess content from across all eight teaching chapters, so there is no paper-by-topic split; Depth carries at least two 6-mark extended-response questions and Breadth carries none. No lesson in this unit makes any paper claim, so nothing needed correcting on that count. No lesson uses 'required practical' language either; this board has Practical Activity Groups (PAG1 reactivity trend, PAG2 electrolysis, PAG3 separation techniques carry this unit's practicals) and no lesson names one wrongly.
tier_rule: Bold content statements only are Higher Tier. In the mapped chapters the Higher-only statements are: C3.2 outcome 6 (biological extraction) and the words 'and ionic equations' in C3.2 outcome 3; C3.3 outcomes 4 (half equations) and 5 (redox as electron transfer); C4.2 outcome 3 and the condensation narrative; C4.5 outcome 3 (redox as electron transfer). C3.4, C4.1, C4.3 and C4.4 contain no bold content at all, so nothing in lessons 3 and 5 is Higher only.

findings.claim: The heading “Biological Methods of Metal Extraction” (n17) sits above the <div class="higher-only"> that holds the whole section.
findings.truth: A Foundation reader gets the heading with nothing under it. The wrapper must open before the heading.
findings.evidence: raw L01 lines 58-60; the same pattern was found in L4 (F10).

findings.claim: Takeaway 3 teaches phytomining and bioleaching, and the exam tip tells every reader to “remember the two named methods”, with no tier flag.
findings.truth: C3.2 outcome 6 (“evaluate alternative biological methods of metal extraction (bacterial and phytoextraction)”) is bold, so it is Higher Tier only. Takeaways take a prefix, never a wrapper.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/chemistry-b-21c-J258-bold.md C3.2 outcome 6, bold.

findings.claim: “Displacement and extraction questions almost always begin with ‘use the reactivity series to explain’.”
findings.truth: An invented claim about how the board words its questions. The advice that follows stands on its own.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the specification's assessment section.

findings.claim: Practice questions 4, 5 and 6 and flashcards 4 and 5 rest on Higher-only content but carry no tier tag.
findings.truth: Q4 and Q5 need phytomining/bioleaching (C3.2.6, bold); Q6 asks for an ionic equation and “and ionic equations” is bold inside C3.2 outcome 3. House convention is “(HT)” on the question type and at the end of a flashcard question.
findings.evidence: bold spec C3.2 outcomes 3 and 6.

findings.claim: Aluminium oxide is described twice as “the ore from which aluminium is extracted by electrolysis”.
findings.truth: Aluminium oxide is a compound purified from the ore bauxite. Lesson 1 of this unit defines an ore as “a rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extraction economically worthwhile”, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: settled fact; L01 glossary term “ore”.

findings.claim: \(Al_2O_3 + C \rightarrow Al + CO_2\) is printed for students to read.
findings.truth: Not balanced: Al 2 to 1, O 3 to 2. It should read 2Al2O3 + 3C → 4Al + 3CO2 (Al 4/4, O 6/6, C 3/3). The point being made — that carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide — is right.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the atom counts.

findings.claim: Flashcards 2 and 6 ask for half-equations with no tier tag.
findings.truth: C3.3 outcome 4 (“write half equations”) and outcome 5 (redox as electron gain or loss) are bold, so both are Higher Tier only. Practice Q5 in the same lesson already carries “(Higher Tier)”, so the lesson is inconsistent with itself.
findings.evidence: bold spec C3.3 outcomes 4 and 5.

findings.claim: “Incomplete combustion also releases sulfur dioxide (if the fuel contains sulfur impurities) and nitrogen oxides (formed at high combustion temperatures when N2 and O2 react)”.
findings.truth: The specification gives incomplete combustion as the source of carbon monoxide and particulates only. Sulfur dioxide comes from burning sulfur impurities and nitrogen oxides from oxidation of nitrogen at high temperature; both happen in complete combustion too. Tying them to incomplete combustion is a misconception stated as fact.
findings.evidence: spec C1.1 outcome 8: “carbon monoxide and particulates (incomplete combustion), sulfur dioxide (combustion of sulfur impurities in fuels), oxides of nitrogen (oxidation of nitrogen at high temperatures...)”.

findings.claim: Knowledge check 2 of the crude oil lesson asks “What is the product at the anode when dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed?”, and the match set repeats it.
findings.truth: The answer key is chemically right (oxygen) but the item belongs to lesson 2. Replaced with a cracking question on this lesson's own content, with the match-set label and answer moved in step.
findings.evidence: raw L03 knowledge_checks [1] and [4]; lesson content covers C3.4 only.

findings.claim: The heading “Condensation Polymerisation” (n14) sits above the <div class="higher-only"> that holds the section.
findings.truth: Same defect as F1: a Foundation reader sees an empty heading. The wrapper must open before the heading.
findings.evidence: raw L04 lines 44-46.

findings.claim: The opening key fact teaches both types of polymerisation to both tiers and says condensation “releases water or HCl as by-product”; takeaway 1 and the exam tip repeat condensation with no tier flag.
findings.truth: C4.2 outcome 3 and the whole condensation narrative are bold, so condensation polymerisation is Higher Tier only. HCl is not a by-product anywhere in this specification: C4.2 names water, formed from the OH of a carboxylic acid monomer and an H atom of the other monomer.
findings.evidence: bold spec C4.2 outcome 3 and narrative.

findings.claim: Practice questions 3 and 4 and flashcards 2 and 3 require condensation polymerisation with no tier tag.
findings.truth: Higher-only content (C4.2 outcome 3, bold). Tagged “(HT)” on the question type and at the end of the flashcard question.
findings.evidence: bold spec C4.2 outcome 3.

findings.claim: Practice question 2 (“Explain why nanoparticles of a substance may behave differently from a large piece”) is typed “3 marks — Explain (HT)”.
findings.truth: Chapter C4.4 contains no bold statements at all, so nothing in it is Higher only. Outcome 2 (“describe the surface area to volume relationship for different-sized particles and describe how this affects properties”) is assessed at both tiers. The tag wrongly tells a Foundation student to skip it.
findings.evidence: bold spec C4.4, no bold outcomes.

findings.claim: Practice question 6 (“Suggest two limitations of using a life cycle assessment”) is typed “2 marks — Short Calculation”.
findings.truth: There is no calculation in the question or the mark scheme. Retyped “2 marks — Suggest”.
findings.evidence: raw L05 practice_questions [5].

findings.claim: “landfill (which conserves resource value but produces methane from decomposing organic material)”.
findings.truth: Landfill loses the resource value of the materials; that loss is the whole argument for recycling, which the same lesson makes two sentences earlier. The sentence teaches the reverse.
findings.evidence: spec C4.5 narrative: recycling breaks products down into materials that are then used to make something else; C4.5 outcome 7 asks learners to evaluate recycling against disposal.

findings.claim: The lesson says “A full LCA considers four stages” and lists extraction, manufacture and packaging, use, end of life. Practice question 4 and its mark scheme repeat the four.
findings.truth: The specification names transport as part of a life cycle assessment. A student who omits it can lose a mark. Transport added to the prose and credited in the mark scheme; the four-stage frame is kept so the rest of the lesson stays consistent.
findings.evidence: spec C4.5 outcome 4a: “the use of water, energy and the environmental impact of each stage in a life cycle, including its manufacture, transport and disposal”.

findings.claim: “In electronics, gold nanoparticles are used in pregnancy tests and rapid diagnostic kits”.
findings.truth: A pregnancy test is not an electronic device. The science in the rest of the sentence is right, so only the framing word changes.
findings.evidence: settled fact: lateral flow tests use colloidal gold, not electronics.

findings.field: content_html (L1 n9; L2 n4 key fact and L2 takeaway n29)
findings.claim: Both-tier body text names which species is oxidised and which is reduced using electron transfer: L1 “the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the metal ion in solution is reduced (gains electrons)”; L2 key fact “cations gain electrons here (reduction)... anions lose electrons here (oxidation)”; L2 takeaway “cations... are reduced; anions... are oxidised”.
findings.truth: The spec is genuinely split here. The bold (Higher-only) statements are C3.3 outcome 5 and C4.5 outcome 3, “explain reduction and oxidation in terms of gain or loss of electrons, identifying which species are oxidised and which are reduced”. But the non-bold narrative of C3.2 already says “the metal in the ore is reduced and carbon is oxidised”, and the non-bold narrative of C3.3 already says ions lose electrons at the anode and gain them at the cathode. Option A: leave as written — each lesson also carries a proper higher-only block for the assessable half-equation work, and the words reduction and oxidation are both-tier. Option B: reword the three passages to keep electron language inside the higher-only blocks, which touches three narration blocks in two lessons. Recommendation: option A, leave it.
findings.evidence: bold spec C3.3 outcome 5 and C4.5 outcome 3 vs the non-bold C3.2 and C3.3 narratives.
findings.ruling: Leave as written: the non-bold C3.2/C3.3 narratives already use oxidised/reduced with electron transfer, so both-tier body text is defensible.

findings.claim: Coverage of the mapped chapters C3 and C4.
findings.truth: Untaught assessable outcomes in the mapped chapters, none of them picked up by the other chemistry units of this subject (checked across chemistry-earth-air-water, chemistry-atoms-patterns-bonding and this unit): C3.4 outcomes 6 and 7 (empirical formula); the whole of C4.1 (quantitative comparison of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals; matching a material to a use; the composition of steel and other alloys, separate science only); C4.3 outcomes 5, 6 and 7 (giant covalent structures; diamond and graphite; allotropes in two and three dimensions); C4.4 outcome 4 (fullerenes and graphene) and outcomes 7, 8 and 9 (standard form, ratios, surface areas and volumes of cubes — the nanoparticle lesson has no calculation at all); C4.5 outcome 1 (corrosion and its prevention by barrier and sacrificial protection, separate science only) and outcome 4c (biodegradable and non-biodegradable materials). Corrosion and the C4.1/C4.3 material-choice content are the largest holes.
findings.evidence: spec C3.4, C4.1, C4.3, C4.4, C4.5; grep of every lesson in the subject for corrosion, sacrificial, diamond, graphene, fullerene, ceramic, composite, alloy, steel, biodegradable, empirical — no hits.

findings.claim: The lesson names the biological methods “phytomining” and “bioleaching” only.
findings.truth: This specification says “bacterial and phytoextraction”. The processes are the same and the lesson's descriptions are accurate, so no edit; a student should recognise the board's own words if they appear in a question.
findings.evidence: spec C3.2 outcome 6.

findings.claim: A full section teaches thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers and covalent cross-links.
findings.truth: None of “thermosetting”, “thermosoftening”, “thermoplastic” or “cross-link” appears in J258. The underlying ideas are in scope — C4.1 outcome 1 lists softening temperature and ease of reshaping, and C4.3 outcome 1 asks about bond strengths and “the ways in which their bonds are arranged” — so the content is defensible and stays. The vocabulary is not the board's.
findings.evidence: grep of the specification: zero hits for all four terms; C4.1 outcome 1 and C4.3 outcome 1.

findings.claim: Cryolite is taught as part of aluminium extraction and is examined in a knowledge check, a flashcard and a 6-mark question.
findings.truth: Cryolite is not named in J258; the spec says only that aluminium oxide is heated to a very high temperature. It is standard teaching, chemically correct and would be credited, so no edit — but it cannot be the load-bearing point of an answer.
findings.evidence: grep of the specification: zero hits for cryolite and bauxite; spec C3.3 narrative.

findings.claim: Knowledge check 3 tests phytomining, which is Higher Tier only.
findings.truth: Knowledge checks carry no tier field, so there is no mechanism to flag this without rewriting the item. The practice questions and flashcards on the same content are now tagged (F4), which is where the tiering matters most.
findings.evidence: bold spec C3.2 outcome 6.

summary: Five lessons, all tier 'both'. The chemistry itself is mostly sound: the reactivity series, the blast furnace equation, both aluminium half equations and their scaling, the molten lead bromide products, the aqueous discharge rules, the copper sulfate worked example, both cracking equations, the poly(ethene) and poly(propene) repeat units, the catalytic-converter equation, the 1-100 nm range and all twenty knowledge-check keys and five match sets recompute or check out. The yield is a wrongly balanced Al2O3 + C equation, aluminium oxide called an ore, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides blamed on incomplete combustion against C1.1 outcome 8, landfill described as conserving resource value, transport missing from the LCA stages the spec names, and an electrolysis knowledge check stranded in the crude oil lesson. The rest is tiering: two higher-only wrappers opened below their headings so Foundation readers saw empty headings, Higher-only content leaking into takeaways and exam tips, ten Higher-only questions and flashcards untagged, and one (HT) tag on chapter C4.4 content that has no bold statements. The largest issue needs no edit: chapters C4.1, C4.3 and C4.5 outcome 1 (corrosion) are barely taught anywhere in this subject.
